stem: How many electrons are in the outer shell of an atom of any Group VII element?

options.rationale: The group number (VII) equals the number of outer-shell electrons.
One outer electron is typical of Group I.
Eight is a full outer shell, as in the noble gases; halogens are one short.
17 is the proton number of chlorine, not its number of outer electrons.

explanation: Halogens are in Group VII, so their atoms have seven outer-shell electrons, for example chlorine 2,8,7. They gain one electron to complete the shell.

stem: How do the melting points of the halogens change from chlorine to iodine?

options.rationale: Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature.
Melting points decrease down Group I, but increase down Group VII.
The change from gas to liquid to solid shows that they rise.
They rise steadily down the group.

explanation: Melting and boiling points increase down Group VII: chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature. The bigger molecules have stronger forces between them.

stem: True or false: the reactivity of the halogens decreases down Group VII.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: chlorine is more reactive than bromine, which is more reactive than iodine.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Reactivity increases down Groups I and II, but decreases down Group VII: chlorine > bromine > iodine.

explanation: Halogen atoms react by gaining an electron. Down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so an electron is gained less easily and reactivity decreases.

stem: Which statement about the volatility of the halogens is correct?

options.content: Volatility decreases down the group, so chlorine is more volatile than iodine.
options.rationale: A volatile substance has a low boiling point; chlorine boils at −34 °C, iodine at 184 °C.

options.content: Volatility increases down the group, so iodine is the most volatile.
options.rationale: Iodine has the highest boiling point of the three, so it is the least volatile.

options.content: All the halogens are equally volatile because they are in the same group.
options.rationale: Their boiling points differ widely.

options.content: Bromine is the least volatile because it is a liquid.
options.rationale: Iodine, a solid, is less volatile than bromine.

explanation: Volatility is how easily a substance turns into a vapour. Boiling points increase down Group VII, so volatility decreases: chlorine (a gas) is the most volatile and iodine (a solid) the least.

stem: Match each halogen with its appearance at room temperature and pressure. One description is not used.
explanation: Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid and iodine a shiny grey-black solid. The colour darkens and the state changes from gas to solid down the group.

stem: Chlorine water is added to colourless potassium bromide solution. What is seen?

options.rationale: Chlorine displaces bromine, which colours the solution orange.
A brown colour shows iodine; there is no iodide here.
Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so a reaction happens.
Both products, potassium chloride and bromine, stay in solution.

explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from the bromide: $\ce{Cl2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + Br2(aq)}$. Bromine in water is orange.
hints: Which is more reactive, chlorine or bromine? What colour is bromine in water?

stem: Which mixture of aqueous solutions reacts?

options.rationale: Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace it.
Chlorine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces it.
Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace it.
Iodine is the least reactive of the three, so it displaces neither.

explanation: A halogen displaces only a **less** reactive halogen from its halide. Chlorine is above iodine, so $\ce{Cl2 + 2KI -> 2KCl + I2}$ happens. In the other three mixtures the halogen is less reactive than the one in the halide, so nothing happens.
hints: A halogen can only displace a halogen below it in the group.

stem: Bromine water is added to colourless sodium iodide solution and the mixture turns brown. Name the two products.

payload.template: The products of the reaction are {{blank:salt}} and {{blank:halogen}}.

explanation: Bromine is more reactive than iodine, so it displaces it: bromine + sodium iodide $\rightarrow$ sodium bromide + iodine, $\ce{Br2(aq) + 2NaI(aq) -> 2NaBr(aq) + I2(aq)}$. Iodine makes the solution brown.

stem: Name the ion formed when a bromine atom gains one electron.

rejected.feedback: Bromine is the element. The ion with a 1− charge is the bromide ion, Br⁻.
The ion of bromine is called the bromide ion.

explanation: A bromine atom has seven outer electrons. Gaining one gives a full outer shell and a $1-$ charge: the **bromide** ion, $\ce{Br-}$.

stem: The boiling points of three halogens are: fluorine $-188\ ^\circ\text{C}$, chlorine $-34\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and iodine $184\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Bromine is a liquid at room temperature ($25\ ^\circ\text{C}$). Which value is the boiling point of bromine?

options.rationale: A boiling point below 25 °C would make bromine a gas at room temperature. (−7 °C is its melting point.)
Between chlorine and iodine, and above room temperature, so bromine is a liquid at 25 °C.
This is lower than chlorine's boiling point, which breaks the trend, and would make bromine a gas.
This is higher than iodine's, but bromine is above iodine, so its boiling point must be lower.

explanation: Boiling points increase down the group, so bromine's must lie between $-34\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $184\ ^\circ\text{C}$. As bromine is a liquid at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$, its boiling point must also be above $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Only $59\ ^\circ\text{C}$ fits.
hints: Bromine lies between chlorine and iodine.
A liquid at 25 °C must boil above 25 °C.

stem: Bromine has proton number 35. How many electrons are there in a bromide ion, $\ce{Br-}$?
explanation: A bromine atom has 35 electrons. A bromide ion has gained one electron: $35 + 1 = 36$.
workedSolution:
1. A neutral bromine atom has 35 protons and 35 electrons.
2. $\ce{Br-}$ has one extra electron: $35 + 1 = 36$.

stem:
A student adds a few drops of each halogen solution to separate test tubes of colourless potassium halide solutions and records the colour of each mixture.

| Halogen solution added | Potassium chloride | Potassium bromide | Potassium iodide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chlorine water (very pale green) | not done | orange | brown |
| Bromine water (orange) | orange | not done | result (b) |
| Iodine solution (brown) | brown | brown | not done |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Bromine water and potassium chloride give an orange mixture. What does this show?

options.rationale: Chlorine would make the mixture very pale green, not orange; and bromine is less reactive.

options.content: There was no reaction: orange is the colour of the bromine water that was added.
options.rationale: Bromine cannot displace the more reactive chlorine.
No reaction has happened, so no new substance forms.
There is no chlorine (element) in this mixture, only chloride ions.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Predict the colour of the mixture of bromine water and potassium iodide.

options.rationale: That would mean no reaction, but bromine is more reactive than iodine.
Iodine is formed, which is coloured.
Bromine displaces iodine, which is brown in solution.
That is the colour of chlorine water.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Chlorine water reacts with potassium bromide solution. Name the two products.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The student repeats the bromine water experiment using sodium iodide instead of potassium iodide. What would she see?

options.content: No change, because sodium is more reactive than potassium.
options.rationale: The metal ion takes no part in a halogen displacement reaction (and sodium is less reactive than potassium).

options.content: An orange colour, because sodium iodide does not react.
options.rationale: Any soluble iodide supplies iodide ions, which bromine oxidises to iodine.

options.content: The same brown colour, because the reaction is between bromine and the iodide ions.
options.rationale: The potassium or sodium ions are spectators: they do not take part.

options.content: A white precipitate of sodium bromide.
options.rationale: Sodium bromide is soluble.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why iodine solution does not react with potassium bromide solution.

points.description: Iodine is less reactive than bromine (it is lower in Group VII)
so it cannot displace bromine from the bromide / a halogen only displaces a less reactive halogen

parts.explanation: Iodine is below bromine in Group VII, so it is less reactive. A halogen can only displace a less reactive halogen from its halide, so iodine cannot displace bromine and the mixture simply stays brown.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Use the results to put chlorine, bromine and iodine in order of reactivity, **most** reactive first.

explanation: A halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its halide. Chlorine displaces bromine (orange) and iodine (brown); bromine displaces only iodine (brown); iodine displaces neither. Where there is no reaction, the mixture just shows the colour of the halogen solution added. The order of reactivity is chlorine > bromine > iodine. The metal ions (potassium or sodium) are spectators.
workedSolution:
1. **(a)** No reaction: the orange colour is just the bromine water.
2. **(b)** Brown (iodine is displaced).
3. **(c)** Potassium chloride and bromine.
4. **(d)** Still brown: only the iodide ions react.
5. **(e)** Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace it.
6. **(f)** Chlorine, bromine, iodine.
hints: Compare each mixture's colour with the colour of the halogen solution that was added.
A halogen only displaces halogens below it in the group.

stem: **Supplement.** Which is the correct ionic equation for the reaction between chlorine and aqueous potassium bromide?

options.rationale: Not balanced: 2 Cl on the left but 1 on the right, and 1 Br on the left but 2 on the right.
Balanced for atoms (2 Cl, 2 Br) and charge (2− on each side); potassium ions are spectators.
This is the reverse reaction: bromine cannot displace the more reactive chlorine.
Potassium ions are spectator ions, and the bromide ions have been left out.

explanation: Full equation: $\ce{Cl2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + Br2(aq)}$. The $\ce{K+}$ ions are unchanged (spectators), so the ionic equation is $\ce{Cl2(aq) + 2Br^-(aq) -> 2Cl^-(aq) + Br2(aq)}$. Check: 2 Cl and 2 Br atoms on each side; total charge $2-$ on each side.
hints: Leave out the ions that do not change.
Check that atoms and charges balance.

stem: **Supplement.** Bromine reacts with iodide ions: $\ce{Br2(aq) + 2I^-(aq) -> 2Br^-(aq) + I2(aq)}$. Which statement is correct?

options.content: Bromine is the reducing agent: it loses electrons and is oxidised.
options.rationale: Bromine gains electrons, so it is reduced; that makes it the oxidising agent.

options.content: Iodide ions gain electrons and are reduced.
options.rationale: Each iodide ion loses an electron to form iodine: it is oxidised.

options.content: No electrons are transferred, so this is not a redox reaction.
options.rationale: Electrons pass from iodide ions to bromine: it is redox.

options.content: Bromine is the oxidising agent: it gains electrons and is reduced.
options.rationale: Each Br atom gains an electron to become Br⁻.

explanation: Bromine gains electrons ($\ce{Br2 + 2e- -> 2Br-}$), so it is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent. Iodide ions lose electrons ($\ce{2I- -> I2 + 2e-}$), so they are oxidised and act as the reducing agent.
hints: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain.
The oxidising agent is the substance that is reduced.

stem: True or false: iodine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not quite: iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace it. There is no reaction.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: iodine is below bromine in Group VII, so it is less reactive and cannot displace it.

explanation: A halogen only displaces a less reactive halogen. Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so no reaction takes place.

stem: Why must experiments that give off chlorine gas be carried out in a fume cupboard?

options.rationale: Chlorine does not burn in air; the hazard is that it is toxic.

options.content: Chlorine is lighter than air and escapes.
options.rationale: Chlorine is denser than air; the reason is its toxicity.

options.content: Chlorine reacts with the light in the laboratory.
options.rationale: The reason is safety: chlorine is toxic.
Chlorine damages the lungs, so the fume cupboard draws it away from people.

explanation: Chlorine (and bromine vapour) are toxic: they attack the lungs and eyes. A fume cupboard removes the gas safely. Wear eye protection as well.

stem:
The table gives information about three halogens.

| Halogen | Melting point / °C | Boiling point / °C | Colour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chlorine | $-101$ | $-34$ | pale yellow-green |
| Bromine | $-7$ | $59$ | red-brown |
| Iodine | $114$ | $184$ | grey-black |

Fluorine is the halogen above chlorine.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Predict the state of fluorine at room temperature.

options.rationale: Fluorine's boiling point must be even lower than chlorine's −34 °C.
Melting points decrease up the group.

options.content: It cannot be predicted from the data.
options.rationale: The trend in boiling point lets you predict it.
Boiling points decrease up the group, and chlorine is already a gas.
That is bromine's colour; colours darken down the group, not up.
Black is predicted for astatine, at the bottom of the group.
Purple is the colour of iodine vapour.
The colours get paler going up the group, so fluorine is paler than chlorine.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: How does the reactivity of fluorine compare with that of chlorine?

options.rationale: Reactivity decreases down the group, so it increases up the group.
Reactivity changes steadily within the group.
Reactivity increases going up Group VII.
Fluorine is the most reactive non-metal of all.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain, in terms of electron shells, why fluorine is more reactive than chlorine.

points.description: A fluorine atom has fewer shells, so its outer shell is closer to the nucleus (less shielding)
so the nucleus attracts an incoming electron more strongly and fluorine gains an electron more easily

parts.explanation: A fluorine atom (2,7) has only two shells, so its outer shell is closer to the nucleus than chlorine's (2,8,7). The nucleus attracts an incoming electron more strongly, so fluorine gains an electron more easily and is more reactive.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Fluorine reacts with sodium to form an ionic compound. Write its formula.

rejected.feedback: Sodium forms Na⁺ and fluorine forms F⁻, so the ratio is 1 : 1: NaF.

explanation: Going up Group VII, melting and boiling points fall, colours get paler and reactivity increases. So fluorine is a pale yellow gas and the most reactive halogen. Its outer shell is closest to the nucleus, so it attracts an extra electron most strongly. It forms F⁻ ions, so sodium fluoride is NaF.
workedSolution:
1. **(a)** Gas.
2. **(b)** Pale yellow.
3. **(c)** More reactive.
4. **(d)** Fewer shells: the outer shell is closer to the nucleus, so an electron is attracted more strongly and gained more easily.
5. **(e)** $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{F-}$: NaF.
hints: Fluorine is at the top of the group: reverse each trend.
Halogens react by gaining one electron.

stem: Hot iron wool is lowered into gas jars of chlorine, bromine vapour and iodine vapour. In chlorine it glows brightly; in bromine vapour it glows less brightly; in iodine vapour it reacts slowly with only a faint glow. What does this show?

options.content: Iodine is the most reactive halogen.
options.rationale: Iodine gives the slowest reaction, so it is the least reactive.

options.content: All three halogens are equally reactive.
options.rationale: The reactions differ clearly in vigour.

options.content: Reactivity decreases from chlorine to bromine to iodine.
options.rationale: The brightest glow shows the fastest, most vigorous reaction.

options.content: Iron is more reactive with iodine because iodine is a solid.
options.rationale: Iodine was used as a vapour, and it reacted least.

explanation: All three halogens react with hot iron to form iron halides (for example $\ce{2Fe + 3Cl2 -> 2FeCl3}$), but the vigour decreases from chlorine to iodine. This confirms that reactivity decreases down Group VII.
hints: A brighter glow means a more vigorous reaction.

stem: Describe the trends in the physical properties of the halogens from chlorine to iodine, and describe how displacement reactions can be used to show their order of reactivity. Include one word or symbol equation. [6]

points.description: Colour darkens down the group (pale yellow-green chlorine, red-brown bromine, grey-black iodine)
State changes from gas to liquid to solid / melting and boiling points increase / volatility decreases
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from a solution of its halide (salt)
A correct example with an observation, for example chlorine water + potassium bromide turns orange (bromine formed), or + potassium iodide turns brown (iodine formed)
A correct word or symbol equation, for example $\ce{Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2}$
Conclusion: reactivity decreases down the group, chlorine > bromine > iodine (iodine displaces neither)

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Down Group VII the colour **darkens**: chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid and iodine a grey-black solid. So the melting and boiling points **increase** and the volatility decreases. The density also increases down the group.

To compare reactivity, add each halogen solution to colourless solutions of potassium chloride, bromide and iodide. A **more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one** from its halide. Chlorine water turns potassium bromide solution **orange**, because bromine forms:

$\ce{Cl2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + Br2(aq)}$

Chlorine also turns potassium iodide brown, and bromine turns potassium iodide brown, but iodine does not react with either chloride or bromide. So reactivity **decreases** down the group: chlorine > bromine > iodine.
answerSpec.markingNotes: Award any six of the seven points.

explanation: Physical trends: darker colours, gas to liquid to solid, higher melting and boiling points, higher density. Displacement results show chlorine > bromine > iodine.
hints: Plan two paragraphs: physical trends, then displacement evidence.

stem:
**Supplement.** Chlorine is bubbled into $50.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of $0.100\ \text{mol/dm}^3$ aqueous potassium iodide until all the iodide has reacted.

$$
\ce{Cl2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + I2(aq)}
$$

($A_r$: I = 127; one mole of any gas occupies $24\ \text{dm}^3$ at r.t.p.)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount, in moles, of potassium iodide used.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of iodine formed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the volume of chlorine, in $\text{cm}^3$ at r.t.p., needed to react with all the iodide.

explanation: Amount of KI $= 0.0500\ \text{dm}^3 \times 0.100\ \text{mol/dm}^3 = 0.00500\ \text{mol}$. The equation shows 2 mol KI give 1 mol $\ce{I2}$, so $n(\ce{I2}) = 0.00250\ \text{mol}$ and its mass is $0.00250 \times 254 = 0.635\ \text{g}$. One mole of $\ce{Cl2}$ reacts per mole of $\ce{I2}$ formed, so $0.00250\ \text{mol}$ of chlorine is needed: $0.00250 \times 24\,000 = 60\ \text{cm}^3$.
hints: Use the mole ratio in the equation: 2 KI give 1 I₂.
